echoes.note: 'Dispersion' (diaspora) is the LXX term for Israel scattered among the nations as covenant curse; Peter recasts the addressees' geographic scatter across Asia Minor as the eschatological diaspora of God's people. High thematic coherence; recurrence of diaspora language across the Deuteronomic curses.

The gathering of the 'dispersed of Judah from the four corners' supplies the restoration backdrop to which 'elect exiles of the dispersion' alludes; faint verbal contact via diaspora, strong thematic coherence with Isaian return-from-exile.

Prayer to 'gather together our dispersion' shows Second Temple use of diaspora as a theological-not-merely-geographic category, the same move Peter makes; Second Temple recurrence supports the reading though no verbal borrowing beyond the term.

Abraham's self-description as a 'stranger and sojourner' (paroikos) is the patriarchal template for the resident-alien identity Peter assigns his readers; the same paroikos/parepidemos word-pair recurs in 1 Peter 2:11. Volume modest, recurrence within the letter high.

'You are strangers and sojourners with me' grounds Israel's tenancy on God's land; Peter universalizes the sojourner status. Faint verbal echo through the sojourner vocabulary, coherent with the letter's pilgrim ecclesiology.
David's 'we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were' is a near-formulaic sojourner confession standing behind 1:1 and 1:17; low volume, supports recurrence.
Election theology—the Most High apportioning peoples and taking Jacob as his allotted portion—underlies 'chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father'; figural/thematic rather than verbal.

'Sanctification... that you may obey... and be sprinkled with his blood' fuses the two halves of Sinai covenant ratification: Israel's pledge 'all that the LORD has spoken we will do and obey' (24:7) and Moses sprinkling the blood of the covenant on the people (24:8). High volume via the obey+blood-sprinkling sequence; thematic coherence with covenant inauguration.

The sprinkling that purifies the unclean (water of the red-heifer ash) is a secondary purification background for 'sprinkled with his blood'; lower volume than Exodus 24, contested as the primary referent.

'I will sprinkle clean water on you... and put my Spirit within you' joins sprinkling with the gift of the Spirit—exactly Peter's pairing of 'sanctification of the Spirit' and 'sprinkled with his blood.' Strong thematic coherence; sprinkling+Spirit recurrence.
Moses sprinkling blood to consecrate the priests supports the priestly-consecration overtone of 'sanctification... sprinkled with his blood,' anticipating the royal priesthood of 2:9. Faint, figural.

'Peace be multiplied to you' (also Daniel 4:1) is the verbatim Aramaic-letter greeting Peter expands to 'grace and peace be multiplied.' Distinctive verbal borrowing of the 'be multiplied' epistolary formula.

'Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel' is the berakah doxology Peter Christianizes as 'Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.' Distinctive opening-blessing form recurring across the Psalter's book-seams.
David's 'Blessed are you, O LORD, the God of Israel our father' supplies both the eulogy form and the Father-language behind 1:3; coherent with the inheritance theme that follows (29:11-16).
'According to your great mercy' echoes the Psalter's 'according to the abundance of your mercy'; low volume but a fixed liturgical collocation.

'The LORD is my portion and my inheritance... a goodly heritage' reframes inheritance from land to God himself, the move behind an 'inheritance kept in heaven.' Thematic coherence high; the imperishable heavenly inheritance transposes the Levitical land-allotment.

The priests have no land-inheritance because 'I am your portion and inheritance'; Peter's heavenly, unfading inheritance figurally fulfills this priestly pattern (cf. royal priesthood, 2:9). Figural, low verbal volume.

'The righteous live forever... they will receive a glorious crown... from the Lord's hand' parallels the imperishable, heaven-reserved inheritance and the 'praise, glory, and honor' of 1:7; Second Temple thematic coherence.

'The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, but the LORD tests hearts' is the proverbial matrix for faith 'tested by fire... more precious than gold.' High thematic coherence; gold-tested-by-fire is a stock wisdom topos Peter applies to faith.

'I will refine them as one refines silver and test them as gold is tested,' set in an eschatological remnant-purification, supplies the trial-as-refinement frame of 1:6-7; verbal contact (refine/test, gold) plus eschatological coherence.
'When he has tested me, I shall come forth as gold' is the closest first-person analogue: testing through suffering yielding vindicated, gold-like faith. Strong thematic coherence, moderate volume.

'My child, when you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing... for gold is tested in the fire, and those found acceptable in the furnace of humiliation.' The fullest pre-Christian template: discipleship + fiery testing + gold + acceptance, mirroring 1:6-7. Second Temple recurrence and high thematic coherence.

'Having been disciplined a little... like gold in the furnace he tried them' joins brief affliction ('a little while', cf. 1:6) with gold-furnace testing of the righteous souls; strong thematic coherence with 1:6-9.

Daniel 'heard but did not understand' and sought the meaning, told the words were 'sealed until the time of the end'—the paradigm for prophets who 'searched diligently... what time the Spirit pointed to' (1:10-11). Distinctive prophet-seeks-yet-defers motif.
'The Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets' undergirds 'to them it was revealed' that they served a later generation (1:12); thematic, low verbal volume.

'The sufferings of Christ and the glories that follow' (1:11) tracks the Servant's affliction-then-vindication arc (Isaiah 52:13-53:12); Peter's signature suffering/glory pattern, faint here but recurrent in the letter.

'Gird up the loins of your mind' literalizes the Passover posture—'your loins girded, your sandals on, in haste'—readiness for imminent deliverance, fitting the redemption-by-the-lamb imagery of 1:18-19. High volume on the distinctive idiom plus contextual Passover coherence.

'Gird up your loins like a man' (also 40:7) is the summons to brace for an encounter with God; supplies the metaphorical (mental readiness) sense Peter intends. Moderate verbal volume; the idiom recurs as a call to resolve.
'Gird up your loins; stand and speak' commissions the prophet to fearless action; reinforces the gird-loins call but is a secondary witness to the idiom. Low distinctiveness.

Formula-marked citation ('because it is written, You shall be holy, for I am holy'). Leviticus 11:44-45 supplies the holiness ground anchored in the exodus ('I am the LORD who brought you up out of Egypt to be your God'), matching Peter's redemption framing. Highest volume—explicit quotation.

'You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy' is the most verbally exact source of 1:16 and heads the Holiness Code chapter Peter draws on repeatedly (love of neighbor, impartiality). Co-primary with Leviticus 11:44-45.

'The God of gods... who is not partial and takes no bribe' is the locus classicus for 'judges impartially, without respect of persons' (1:17). Distinctive 'shows no partiality' formula; high thematic coherence.
'You repay each according to his work' supplies the second half of 1:17 (judges 'according to each one's work'); a fixed retributive formula. Moderate volume, recurs widely.
'I the LORD... give to each according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds' parallels the judge-by-works formula; secondary witness, low distinctiveness.
'The Lord is judge, and with him there is no partiality' shows the impartial-judge formula in Second Temple piety, supporting the recurrence of 1:17's idea; minimal verbal borrowing.

'You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money' stands behind 'redeemed, not with silver or gold' (1:18)—redemption explicitly not monetary. Distinctive silver/gold-vs-true-redemption contrast.

'I will redeem you with an outstretched arm' is the exodus redemption verb Peter applies to ransom 'from the futile ways inherited from your fathers'—a new exodus from ancestral bondage. Thematic coherence high.

'Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, worthless things (vanity) in which there is no profit' closely matches 'the futile ways inherited from your fathers' (1:18)—ancestral idolatry as vanity. Notable verbal contact (inherited+vain+fathers).

'Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male a year old' is the Passover-lamb specification behind 'a lamb without blemish or spot' (1:19), reinforcing the redemption/exodus matrix of the pericope. High volume on the without-blemish lamb.

'Like a lamb that is led to the slaughter... he opened not his mouth' supplies the suffering-Servant lamb whose blood ransoms; Peter fuses Passover lamb with Isaian Servant (cf. the dense Isaiah 53 citation in 2:22-25). High thematic coherence and recurrence in the letter.
The sacrificial requirement that an offering be 'without blemish... no defect' generalizes the spotless-lamb language of 1:19 across the cult. Supports volume of the blemish-free motif.

'My servant shall be exalted and lifted up' grounds 'raised him from the dead and gave him glory' (1:21)—the Servant's vindication. Faint, figural, but coherent with Peter's suffering-then-glory pattern.

'Love one another earnestly from the heart' (1:22) draws on the Holiness Code command 'you shall love your neighbor as yourself'—the same Leviticus 19 chapter Peter quotes for holiness in 1:16. Recurrence within the source chapter supports the link though Peter rephrases.
'Living and abiding word of God' resonates with oaths by 'him who lives forever'; faint, the enduring/living quality is better anchored in the Isaiah 40 citation that follows.

Verbatim, formula-introduced citation ('For, All flesh is like grass... the grass withers, the flower falls, but the word of the Lord endures forever'). Peter quotes the LXX of Isaiah 40:6-8 to ground the imperishable seed/word; highest volume. Isaiah's word-of-comfort frames the whole exile-and-restoration ecclesiology of the letter.

'As for man, his days are like grass; he flourishes like a flower of the field; the wind passes over it and it is gone' is a parallel grass/flower-frailty topos reinforcing the Isaiah 40 quotation. Moderate volume; same withering-flower imagery.

'Why are you afraid of mortal man... who fades like grass?' is a nearby Isaian grass-frailty saying within the same comfort-of-Zion section, supporting the Isaiah 40 recurrence. Low distinctiveness on its own.

Humanity 'like grass that is renewed in the morning... in the evening it fades and withers' is another grass-mortality witness underlining the perishable-vs-enduring contrast of 1:23-25. Faint, thematic.
